title: Elektra
full_review:
"Elektra" (20th Century Fox) is anything but Elektra-fying.

The low-wattage action movie is based on the titular Marvel Comics character (played by a buff Jennifer Garner of "Alias" fame), a blade-wielding femme fatale who runs afoul of a super-powered crime syndicate when she decides to turn from her assassin ways and protect the two targets -- a young girl (newcomer Kirsten Prout) and her father (Goran Visnjic) -- whom she has been contracted to kill.

Terence Stamp plays Stick, a mystical blind master who instructs Elektra in the warrior ways (think Master Po of the old "Kung Fu" TV series with a dry British accent).

Sporting a chiseled physique, the sultry Garner glistens with star appeal but, unfortunately, her role consists mostly of stalking through the film in brooding hellcat mode, striking menacing poses in tight-fitting outfits. A perpetually clenched jaw is all that passes for the reluctant assassin's inner moral conflict.

Garner reprises the role she played in 2003's equally dismal "Daredevil" starring Ben Affleck, in which her character fell in love with the costumed crime fighter's alter ego, Matt Murdock.

Directed by Rob Bowman, the spinoff adds up to little more than a series of frenetic and violent death duels sloppily strung together in a hackneyed attempt to distract viewers from the lame dialogue, muddled plot and lack of emotion which do not even provide much in the way of B-movie thrills.

The film contains recurring strong stylized violence, including several impalings and an implied decapitation, thematic moral ambiguities, a gratuitously erotic same-sex kiss, sporadic crude language and an instance of profanity. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is L -- limited adult audience, films whose problematic content many adults would find troubling. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents are strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.
